# Aggañña Sutta (DN 27 (PTS DN iii 80))

**ID:** DN 27 (PTS DN iii 80)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Aggañña Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Origin of the World
**PTS:** DN iii 80
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn27
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Aggañña Sutta* (DN 27; PTS DN iii 80) is the twenty-seventh discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. Addressed to the former brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, the sutta responds to Brahmanical claims of intrinsic ritual purity and caste superiority by offering a naturalistic, co-dependent account of cosmic and social evolution [SuttaCentral; Macy 1978; Williams 2005a]. Over more than half the discourse, the Buddha narrates an aetiological genesis account: as the universe expands after a period of cosmic contraction, luminous and immaterial beings from the Ābhassara realm gradually fall into corporeal embodiment after consuming the essence of the earth (*paṭhavī-rasa*) [Collins 1998; Williams 2005a]. The arising of bodily differences leads to arrogance, gender differentiation, sexual desire, agriculture, and private property, which in turn breeds theft and conflict, necessitating the election of the first monarch (*Mahāsammata*) to establish social order [Collins 1998]. The text lampoons Brahmanical etymologies—such as humorously defining Vedic students (*ajjhāyaka*) as "non-meditators" who compose (*ganthe*) hymns—and characterizes the Tathāgata with the designations *dhammaja*, *dhammabhūta*, and *dhammakāya* [Jantrasrisalai 2008; Williams 2005b]. It culminates in the soteriological principle that members of any class who restrain body, speech, and mind and develop the factors of awakening can attain parinibbāna [Gethin 2001].

Scholars such as Konrad Meisig have analyzed the composite structure of the sutta in relation to its parallels, noting that the aetiological myth may have circulated independently [Gethin 2001; Williams 2005a]. Curated parallels include three Chinese translations—DĀ 5, MĀ 154, and T 10 (which Meisig identifies under titles concerning the four *varṇa*s or discourses to Vāsiṣṭha and Bhāradvāja)—as well as Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta65, SF 277), the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (3.104), and Vinaya lineages such as the *Mahāvastu* and *Saṅghabhedavastu* [SuttaCentral; Gethin 2001; Williams 2005a]. DharmaNexus independently confirms these alignments, finding dense correspondences with the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* and *Saṅghabhedavastu*, Tibetan translations of the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D 4094) and *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D 3), and Chinese versions in T 26, T 10, and T 1 [DharmaNexus]. In Pali-internal reuse, DharmaNexus identifies substantial overlaps with discourses refuting caste prejudice, notably the *Assalāyana Sutta* (MN 93) and *Madhura Sutta* (MN 84), as well as cosmological passages in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* (DN 1) [DharmaNexus]. In later Buddhist literature, the cosmological framework of DN 27 was extracted and incorporated into works such as the *Visuddhimagga*, *Lokapaññatti*, and *Cakkavāḷadīpanī* [Norman 1983; Macy 1978].
